title: Where things are and what happened

grammarPoints.title: あります and います
grammarPoints.meaning: Use あります for the existence or location of inanimate things and plants, and います for people and animals. The same pattern can express that someone possesses something or that an event is scheduled.
grammarPoints.formation: Existence: place に entity が あります／います. Possession: (person は) entity が あります／います. Events: place で event が あります, with a time expression when needed.
notes: The entity that exists is marked が; the location is marked に.
Use います for living people and animals, あります for objects, plants, and events.
In the possession use, が marks what someone has; do not confuse this with the location pattern.
An event can be described with あります, such as a meeting or concert taking place.

grammarPoints.title: Location words
grammarPoints.meaning: Describe a known person or thing by giving its position relative to a landmark. Japanese position words are nouns linked to the landmark with の.
grammarPoints.formation: X は Y の position です. A location can also be expressed as Y の position に X が あります／います. Between: X は Y と Z の間です.
notes: Use の between a landmark and 上／下／中／前／後ろ／右／左／近く／隣.
隣 usually relates two people or two buildings; do not freely use it for mismatched objects.
With an action at that relative place, use で. 前 can describe a position across the street; 後ろ is behind, and 裏 can suggest a hidden back side.

grammarPoints.title: Past tense of です
grammarPoints.meaning: でした identifies a past state or identity. The polite negative past says something was not the stated category.
grammarPoints.formation: Noun + でした; noun + じゃなかったです or じゃありませんでした for the negative past. The latter is more formal.
notes: でした is the past counterpart of です.
じゃなかったです is common polite conversation; じゃありませんでした is more formal.
This point concerns noun predicates; adjective past forms are taught later.

grammarPoints.title: Past tense of verbs
grammarPoints.meaning: Polite past verb forms describe completed actions. The negative past says that an action did not happen.
grammarPoints.formation: Verb ます-stem + ました for past affirmative; verb ます-stem + ませんでした for past negative.
notes: Japanese verbs do not change for the subject.
The past ending comes at the end of the sentence after objects, locations, and time phrases.
Do not confuse the past verb endings with past noun predicate でした.

grammarPoints.title: も with other particles
grammarPoints.meaning: も can mark an additional item or place. With many particles it follows the particle; in topic, subject, and direct-object roles it commonly replaces は, が, or を.
grammarPoints.formation: Additional direct object: noun + も + verb. Additional location/destination: noun + にも／でも／へも + verb. Interpret the extra item as sharing the same action or relation in context.
notes: Use も only when an earlier parallel action or relation is understood.
For an object marked を, replace を with も. With に, で, or へ, put も after the particle.

grammarPoints.title: Duration expressions
grammarPoints.meaning: A duration phrase says how long an activity continues. ぐらい after the duration means about that long.
grammarPoints.formation: [duration] (ぐらい) + verb. A simple duration does not take に. Add 半 after 時間, as in 一時間半 (one and a half hours); ぐらい follows 半.
notes: Do not add に after a length of time in this duration pattern.
Distinguish a duration like 三時間 from a clock time like 三時, which normally takes に.
ぐらい follows the duration phrase.

grammarPoints.title: たくさん with verbs
grammarPoints.meaning: たくさん describes a large number or amount. It can go before the object noun or after its particle, before the verb. The same two positions work in existence sentences.
grammarPoints.formation: たくさん object を verb, or object を たくさん verb. Existence: たくさん entity が あります／います, or entity が たくさん あります／います.
notes: These exercises practise the adverbial pattern without の.
Distinguish a large quantity from simply doing the same action frequently; context gives the intended reading.

grammarPoints.title: と for noun lists and companions
grammarPoints.meaning: と joins nouns as a complete list meaning ‘and’; after a person it can mark a companion, meaning ‘with’. Context distinguishes the uses.
grammarPoints.formation: List: noun A と noun B + predicate. Companion: person + と + activity verb.
notes: The list use presents the named items as the whole set; it does not mean ‘and so on’.
In the companion use, と marks the person who participates with the subject.
Do not confuse this companion marker with で, which marks the means or place of an action.
